title: The hyperinvariant subspace problem
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: OpenAI's negative answer (2026) to the hyperinvariant subspace problem: every infinite-dimensional separable complex Hilbert space carries a nonzero operator S with ||S^n||^(1/n) -> 0 whose commutant is a proper, weakly closed, unital, transitive algebra; so S has no hyperinvariant subspace other than 0 and the whole space, and the transitive algebra problem has a negative answer too. The first lesson proves Domar's theorem that a bilateral weighted shift whose logarithmic weights are regular and decay at a quadratic rate has only the tails as invariant subspaces (convex minorants, support separation), for l^2 and in Domar's one-sided form. The second builds a measurable field of such shifts over the 2-adic integers with the odometer, proves that operators commuting with the scalar multipliers are fields of operators, and proves ||S^n|| <= exp(-10 floor((n+1)^2/4)). The third constructs a contraction commuting with S that moves every tail one step backward along the odometer, using opposite logarithmic drifts at the two ends of the fibres, and proves transitivity by a strict-descent argument on a probability space. It also lists the invariant subspaces of S and the multipliers and shows that finitely many polar conjugates of |S| generate an atomic algebra while all of them generate a diffuse one.
prerequisites: foundations-of-von-neumann-algebras lessons hilbert-spaces-and-compact-operators (Theorems 2.2 and 2.3, projection and Riesz-Frechet theorems; Theorem 4.1, orthonormal bases; Theorem 5.1, compact operators; Theorem 9.1, multiplication operators), the-double-commutant-theorem (Proposition 2.1 and Definition 2.3; Section 9, the uniqueness lemma for measures and the product of probability spaces), the-spectral-theorem-for-bounded-self-adjoint-operators (Lemma 1.1, Theorem 3.1)
harmonic-analysis-on-locally-compact-groups lesson measure-and-hilbert-space-tools (Theorems 2.1 and 2.2, monotone convergence, Fatou and dominated convergence; Theorem 3.2, completeness of L^2)
